client: I've been having a really hard time since losing my partner in the accident six months ago. Things I used to love, like hiking or cooking new recipes, just feel completely hollow now, like I'm going through the motions without any real feeling behind it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I guess I'm here because I don't know what else to do.
therapist: What you've been carrying these past six months — the loss, the emptiness where joy used to live — that's an enormous weight, and it makes complete sense that even things you loved now feel distant. I also want to gently acknowledge the courage it took to show up here, even with that doubt that it might not help, because that small act of reaching out often matters more than it feels like it does in the moment. Can you tell me a little more about what a typical day looks like for you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: A typical day is pretty bleak, honestly. I wake up and for just a split second I forget, and then it all comes crashing back and I just kind of lie there, not really wanting to get up. I eventually do the basics — eat something, maybe go for a walk — but it all feels mechanical, like I'm just running out the clock until I can go back to sleep.
therapist: That moment you describe — that split second of forgetting before it all rushes back — sounds like one of the most painful parts of the day, almost like losing him again each morning. What you're describing, going through the motions and waiting for the day to end, is something many people experience in grief, and it tells me how much energy this loss is taking just to survive right now. I'm wondering, on those walks you mentioned, is there ever even a flicker of something — a moment that feels slightly less mechanical — or does it all feel equally flat?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: There was one moment last week, actually — I walked past this bakery and the smell hit me, and for maybe five seconds I felt something, I'm not sure what exactly, maybe just... present, I guess. But then I immediately felt guilty about it, like how dare I have even a moment of something good when he's gone. It's like any tiny break from the grief feels like a betrayal.
therapist: That moment at the bakery — feeling present for just a few seconds — is actually really significant, and the guilt that rushed in right after makes a lot of sense, even though it's also worth gently questioning. That guilt is rooted in a kind of loyalty and love, but grief doesn't require you to suffer every single moment to prove how much he mattered to you. I'm curious — do you think he would have wanted those five seconds of presence to feel like a betrayal to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: No, he wouldn't have wanted that — he was always the one pushing me to enjoy things, to slow down and actually taste the food or notice the view. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling okay about it are two completely different things, and I think that's where I get stuck. It's like I can reason my way to the right answer but my gut just doesn't believe it yet.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it — and that's actually at the heart of so much of what we'd work on together. It's almost like you're describing him so vividly there, someone who wanted you to actually *be* in your life, not just move through it. What do you think it would take for your gut to start catching up, even just a little, to what your head already knows?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I don't know — and that uncertainty itself feels overwhelming sometimes. I think part of me is almost afraid to close that gap, like if I start actually feeling okay, it means I'm moving on, and moving on feels like leaving him behind. I'm not sure therapy can fix that fear, because it's not really a thinking problem, it's more like... I'd have to want to let go a little, and I'm not sure I'm ready for that.
therapist: What you just said — that healing feels like abandonment — is one of the most common and most painful places people get stuck in grief, and it takes real honesty to name it so clearly. I want to offer a gentle reframe: moving forward doesn't mean leaving him behind, it means learning to carry him with you differently, the way he'd want to be carried — in those moments of tasting something good or noticing a view. You don't have to be ready to let go right now; can we just stay curious together about what it might mean to *keep* him while also slowly letting yourself back in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That framing of "carrying him differently" is actually... I don't know, it doesn't feel as threatening as I expected it to when you put it that way. But I'm also a little skeptical, because it sounds almost too neat, like a nice idea that might not hold up when I'm actually standing in my kitchen at 7pm and the loneliness just hits like a wall. I guess I'm willing to stay curious, like you said, but I'm not sure how that translates into anything real on a Tuesday night when it's just me and the silence.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely fair — "carrying him differently" has to mean something real at 7pm on a Tuesday, not just sound good in a therapy session. One small, concrete thing we could explore is this: when that wall of silence hits, instead of trying to push through it or distract from it, what if you let yourself deliberately bring *him* into that moment — maybe the way he'd have commented on what you were cooking, or something he would have said. It's not about performing grief or forcing feeling, but about practicing his presence rather than only feeling his absence — would something like that feel worth trying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually does resonate with me more than I expected, because he had this habit of narrating everything he cooked like he was on a cooking show, and just thinking about that made me almost smile and then immediately want to cry. But I worry that if I deliberately try to conjure him up like that, it'll feel forced or artificial, like I'm just playing pretend instead of it being real. What if I do it and it just feels hollow, and then I've somehow made it worse?
therapist: That image of him narrating his cooking like a show host — the fact that it brought you almost to a smile even as it brought tears — that's not hollow, that's him, still vivid and real inside you. The worry that deliberately accessing that might feel forced is worth holding lightly, because there's actually no wrong way to do it — if it feels hollow one night, that's just information, not failure, and if it brings that bittersweet almost-smile, that's him still with you. What if the goal wasn't to make it feel a certain way, but just to let whatever comes up, come up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Taking the pressure off it feeling a certain way does make it seem less daunting, I'll admit that. I think my fear was that I'd grade myself on how well I did it, and if it came out wrong I'd feel like I'd somehow failed him on top of everything else. Maybe I could try it once this week, just once, without any expectations — though I'm already a little nervous about what might come up if I actually let myself go there.
therapist: The nervousness you're feeling about trying this is actually a really healthy sign — it means you're taking it seriously and that it matters to you, which makes sense given how much he matters to you. That instinct to grade yourself is so worth noticing, because it sounds like it shows up in a lot of places, turning even moments of connection into tests you could fail. Just once, no grade, no right or wrong — and whatever comes up, whether it's tears or an almost-smile or just silence, we can talk about it together next time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The grading myself thing — I hadn't really connected that to grief specifically, but you're right that it's kind of everywhere in my life, and hearing it named like that was a little uncomfortable in a way that felt true. I think I can try the once-this-week thing, but I want to be honest that part of me is already looking for an exit ramp, like I'll get to Tuesday and tell myself it's not the right moment or I'm too tired. How do I not let myself off the hook without it turning into another thing to grade myself on?
therapist: The fact that you're already anticipating the exit ramp and naming it out loud is actually you holding yourself accountable in the healthiest possible way — that's not avoidance, that's self-awareness. One gentle idea: rather than waiting for Tuesday to feel like the *right* moment, what if you picked a specific, small anchor ahead of time — like after you've eaten something, you let yourself say one thing out loud that he would have said — so it's less a decision to make in the moment and more just something that's already decided. And if you do let yourself off the hook one night, the question isn't "did I fail" but "what got in the way" — that's the version of accountability that doesn't turn into another grade.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The specific anchor idea actually helps, because you're right that if I leave it open-ended I'll just keep waiting for a moment that feels ready and it never will. I think after dinner makes sense, because that was always when he'd be loudest in the kitchen anyway. I'm still a little scared, but it's a smaller scared than when we started talking today, which I guess is something.
therapist: "A smaller scared" is real progress, and the fact that you've already connected the anchor to *his* specific moment — the loudest time in the kitchen — tells me this isn't abstract for you, it's already becoming something true. You came in today not sure talking would change anything, and you're leaving with something small and concrete that belongs to both of you. I'll be thinking of you after dinner this week.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
